title: Adaptive cost profiles and cache policy experimental memo
body:
Purpose:
This memo captures an experimental set of recommended runtime settings (batching, KV cache retention, and quantization) plus a compact cost model sketch for running small-to-medium production workloads. The goal is to maximize unit-cost reduction while bounding latency regressions and preserving output quality. This is intentionally opinionated and conservative — meant to serve as an A/B rollout plan and checklist rather than a final policy doc.

Context and constraints:
- We expect heterogeneous request patterns: chat-like sessions (long, interactive), short completions (single-turn UI), and high-throughput embedding/rerank pipelines.
- Target models: open-weights 7B–13B family and quantized 13B variants. Also include our curated 70B-compatible variants for Dedicated customers.
- Operational limits: per-tenant memory caps, token throughput SLOs (p95 latency targets), and safety/quality guardrails.
- Safety-first: any setting that shows >3% absolute degradation on critical eval suite triggers rollback.

High-level recommendation summary (one-line):
Adopt per-endpoint adaptive batching profiles, tiered KV-cache retention with explicit memory budgets, and model-specific quantization profiles with automated fallback thresholds. Phase rollout with short canary windows and continuous evals.

1) Adaptive batching profiles (per-route configuration)
Rationale: A single global batch size over-provisions for latency-sensitive endpoints or leaves throughput on the table for bulk workers. We propose three profiles with explicit knobs that the serving runtime already supports.
Profiles (recommended starting parameters):
- low-latency: target_batch_size=8, max_wait_ms=10, concurrency_cap=4 -> intended for interactive UI endpoints where p95 latency matters. Expect ~5–12% cost reduction vs no-batching on short sequences, usually neutral for tail latency.
- balanced: target_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=25, concurrency_cap=8 -> default for most chat flows; balances latency and throughput; expect ~20–35% token-cost reduction depending on sequence length distribution.
- throughput: target_batch_size=128, max_wait_ms=80, concurrency_cap=32 -> for offline or background tasks (reranking, embeddings). Acceptable p95 latency is higher; expect ~40–65% cost reduction.
Operational notes:
- Use adaptive backpressure: when GPU-utilization >75% switch routes to throughput profile automatically (policy configurable).
- Add request hints: clients can signal latency_tier to help routing.
- Expose per-route metrics: average batch size, max_wait_ms distribution, dropouts due to concurrency cap.

2) Hierarchical KV cache retention policy
Rationale: KV cache hits are the cheapest token path; retention policy controls memory footprint and hit-rate. Uniform long retention wastes GPU memory for many short sessions.
Tiers (recommended):
- transient (default) — retention=30s, target hit-rate for casual single-turn traffic. Memory budget: small, circular. Good for SMS/chat-bots.
- session — retention=10min, intended for multi-turn interactive sessions; expect higher hit-rate for real chat flows. Memory budget: per-tenant session entries limited; evict least-recently-used across sessions.
- persistent-prefix — retention=24h (or configurable), only for pinned/conversational prefixes (e.g., system prompts, company-provided context) that many requests reuse. Stored compressed (variable-length) with explicit quotas per tenant.
Metrics to monitor:
- cache_hit_rate (per-model, per-endpoint), average_kv_memory_bytes, eviction_count, per-tenant quota_utilization.
Tradeoffs: 24h retention gives large hit-rate gains for assistant-style workloads (30–50% token savings) but increases memory cost and increases warmup complexity on node failover. Start with conservative per-tenant persistent quotas.

3) Quantization profiles with safety fallbacks
Rationale: Quantization delivers large cost wins but model and workload sensitivity varies. We suggest shipping multiple quant profiles per model and selecting at inference-time by route workload tags.
Recommended profile tiers (examples):
- fp16 (baseline, no quant) — gold standard for quality-sensitive customers.
- q8a (8-bit asymmetric) — safe general-purpose profile; minimal measured eval drift (<1% on our regression set), ~1.6–2x speedup and memory reduction.
- q4h / q4_0 — good for 7B/13B where larger speedups enable denser packing; measured eval drift 1–3% depending on prompt length.
- mixed (q4 + fp16 critical layers) — experimental for high-value endpoints that need some quality preservation while reaping memory benefits.
Guidelines and fallback thresholds:
- Per-model baseline eval: compute baseline metrics on reference eval suite (P0 prompts, safety checks).
- Acceptable drift: <=2% absolute on primary metric (e.g., exact match/ROUGE). If exceeded, restrict profile to canary traffic or remove.
- Runtime monitor: compare downstream quality regression signals (customer-chosen prompts, embeddings drift) and if alert rate > threshold (default 0.5% of requests flagged) automatically revert to higher-precision profile for that tenant/route.

4) Compact cost model overview (spreadsheet sketch)
We maintain a short spreadsheet (linked above) that models per-token cost for combinations of: model, quant-profile, batch profile, KV-hit-rate, average sequence length. Columns (sheet):
- route_name, model, quant_profile, batch_profile, kv_hit_rate, avg_seq_len, tokens_per_sec, p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1M_tokens (USD), relative_cost_vs_baseline (%)
Formulas (high-level):
- effective_tokens_served = total_tokens * (1 - kv_hit_rate) + kv_hit_rate * cached_cost_factor
- compute_cost = gpu_unit_price_per_sec * (inference_seconds_per_1M_tokens)
- inference_seconds_per_1M_tokens derived from measured tokens_per_sec under the profile.
Notes:
- We recommend running a two-week synthetic backtest on recent logs to estimate batch size distributions and KV-hit-rates per route before committing profile defaults.

5) Rollout plan and guardrails
Phased rollout (recommended):
- Stage 0: lab benchmark on representative models + 5 synthetic traffic shapes (1 day runs).
- Stage 1: internal canary (service-level) with 5% traffic for 24–72 hours. Monitor latency, cost delta, eval drift.
- Stage 2: customer opt-in pilot (select customers with high instrumentation) for 2–4 weeks.
- Stage 3: wider opt-in then default changes for low-risk routes after 6 weeks of stable metrics.
Guardrails/triggers for automatic rollback:
- p95 latency increase >10% on low-latency routes.
- Quality metric absolute degradation >3% on primary eval suite.
- Error rate increase >0.5% or latency SLO violations spike.
- Cache memory utilization exceeding budget for >10 minutes.

6) Monitoring and dashboards (must-have metrics)
- per-route: avg_batch_size, max_wait_ms_p90, kv_hit_rate, tokens_per_sec, p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1M_tokens
- per-tenant: persistent_kv_quota_util, quant_profile_in_use, rollback_events_count, eval_drift_rate
- alerting: automated alert when eval_drift_rate > 0.5% or cache_quota_util > 90% for more than 5 minutes

Action items (next 10 working days):
- Aisha: spin up synthetic backtest using last 14 days of logs and produce a per-route batch-size histogram (due: +5 days).
- Jon: prototype persistent-prefix cache quota enforcement in the node agent (PR + basic tests) (due: +7 days).
- Lina: add quant-profile tagging to model catalog and surface simple fallback toggles in the Console (UI/UX sketch) (due: +10 days).
- Ethan: create canary dashboard and wire basic alerts for the three guardrail triggers (due: +6 days).

Open questions and risks:
- Multi-tenant fairness: how to prioritize high-value tenants when memory/batch contention occurs? (policy design needed).
- Long-tail prompts: quant sensitivity increases for some prompt types — need a targeted prompt-level eval harness.
- Node failover: persistent-prefix caches will warm slowly on node churn; need warm-start strategies (preload top prefixes).

Appendix: quick test checklist for engineers
- reproduce cost model numbers locally for a sample route (script + sample logs)
- run quant-profile A/B with 1k prompts from the eval harness and record primary metric deltas
- enable persistent-prefix on a single tenant with 1GB quota and observe eviction patterns over 48 hours

Closing note:
This is a working draft focused on practical, low-friction changes that can yield measurable unit-cost wins. The intention is to land a small set of safe defaults (balanced profile + session KV + q8a profile) while enabling opt-in aggressive settings for throughput-sensitive customers. Feedback welcome — particularly from SRE and serving-runtime on the feasibility of adaptive concurrency caps and memory accounting for persistent prefixes.
summary: Draft recommendations for per-route adaptive batching, hierarchical KV cache retention, and model quantization profiles plus a compact cost model and phased rollout plan.
